headline: New moon springs load up Stratford Shoal as fluke push out of the warm bays
subhead: Central Sound stripers and blues are keying on the building tide while fluke abandon the overheated flats for cooler inlet water.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it usually does in early July — it split into two different fisheries depending on which side of the rip you were standing on. A few days of northeast wind kept upwelling going along the eastern approaches, holding Stratford Shoal and the water off Middle Ground Light noticeably cooler than the bays tucked in behind Oyster Bay and the Norwalk Islands. Those inner bays have been creeping into the upper 70s, and that temperature split is doing more to organize the bite right now than any single tide or moon phase. Bait doesn't like 78-degree water any more than gamefish do, and both have been sliding toward the cooler edges — the channels, the inlets, the rips where current keeps things mixed.

This week the moon goes new around the 11th-13th, and that means building spring tides through the weekend — bigger swings, more current, more water moved on every stage. For Central Sound that's a big deal because our structure — Stratford Shoal, the Norwalk Islands rock piles, Charles Island — all depends on current to stack bait against something solid. The best alignment I'm watching is the PM flood pushing into sunset Friday through Monday. That's the first evening high-tide window we've had line up with dusk since the June full moon, and historically that's when the bigger fish in this zone decide to feed instead of just cruise. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't blow the surface into chop, I'd have my rod in the water for that window over anything else this week.

Striper fishing has been real but it's work, not a gimme. The Stratford Shoal rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent — bass in the 24 to 34-inch range on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 25 to 40 feet, and a few better fish, high 30s, coming off live-lined bunker snagged right off the surface schools near the Shoal buoy. Bucktails — 1.5 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of pork rind or a white Gulp swimming mullet — have worked the drift along the rock edges off the Norwalk Islands on the last of the incoming, especially around Sheffield Island and the Cockenoe Reef complex. Nothing has been stacked thick. You're picking off two or three quality fish a trip if you put in the time and hit the tide right, not backing into a blitz.

Bluefish have been the more reliable action for guys who just want bent rods. Peanut bunker showed up thick around Charles Island and the outer Norwalk Islands over the last week, and the blues have been all over them on the tide change — surface blitzes early and late in the day, poppers and metal getting hit almost as soon as they land. Nothing giant, mostly 2 to 4 pounds, but if you want a guaranteed bend in the rod that's your play right now, especially the first hour of light off Charles Island before the boat traffic picks up.

Fluke are the interesting story this week because the pattern has genuinely shifted. The warm bay water — I've heard numbers close to 79 degrees in the shallow flats off Oyster Bay and Huntington — has pushed the better fluke out of the bay and into the channels and inlet mouths where the water stays cooler and better oxygenated. Port Jefferson Harbor's outer channel and the mouth of the Eatons Neck cut have both been holding fish in 30 to 40 feet on the outgoing tide. Standard drift with 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, or plain bait rigs with squid strips, has been the ticket. Fish to 5 pounds have come out of that deeper water, though the average fish is closer to 18 to 20 inches — solid eating fish, not doormats. If you've been fishing the shallow flats all June and getting nothing, this is the week to run out to the deeper structure instead.

Porgies remain the honest bread-and-butter fish of the zone. Middle Ground Light and the rock piles around Stratford Shoal are holding good numbers, and a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clam strips in 20 to 35 feet on either tide will keep a cooler full. Nothing flashy, but it's the most reliable thing going in Central Sound right now.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are still a no-show. Water temps have been above the old 70-degree threshold for over two weeks now and I haven't heard of a single fish. That old rule of thumb about weakfish showing once the water warms just isn't holding up anymore — necessary, apparently, but not enough on its own. I'd stop planning trips around it.

As for bonito — it's too early for Central Sound. That corridor is spreading out east right now, Newport down through Point Judith and the Block Island edges, and the real push into our waters typically doesn't happen until August when the bait funnels through the narrows. Worth watching, not worth a special trip yet.

Looking ahead, I'm circling Friday through Monday for the evening flood at Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands. Big spring tide, sunset alignment, cooler water still holding bait against structure — that's the recipe. If the wind cooperates I expect a better grade of striper to show up on that tide than what we've seen through the neap stretch. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is the fluke drift off Eatons Neck — that pattern's been steady enough to fall back on.
